text: to thank the representative from Kabadi
for delivering that statement in Kabadi
Creole.
>> His Excellency Vasile Topan, Prime
Minister of the Republic of Moldova,
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Vice President,
Deputy Secretary General, Excellencies,
ladies and gentlemen, this summer, the
Republic of Muldova turned 35. For much
of that time, the world described us as
a country caught between east and west,
a place where others decided.
I stand here at the new prime minister
of a country that has decided.
Small countries do not choose their
geography or their size. But small does
not mean powerless.
Nations like people are shaped by the
choices they make, whom they trust, whom
they elect, whom they call friends, and
how they respond when things turn
against them.
For a long time, others made many of
those choices for us.
Soviet authorities deported our families
to Siberia, forced our Romanian language
into another alphabet, and told us it
had another name. After independence,
Moscow used gas and trade restrictions
as leverage over our country. Step by
step, we began choosing for ourselves.
Romanian is again written in Latin and
spoken freely.
Governments change peacefully at the
ballot box and when our democracy was
threatened, Muldovans have defended it
through elections and civic action.
We also reduced Russia's economic
leverage on us. We diversified our gas
purchases. In just five years,
renewables grew from nothing to around
30% of our energy supply. Our
electricity system is increasingly
integrated with Romania and the European
grid and our companies sell on some of
the most demanding markets in Europe and
the world.
But the Kremlin kept trying. Muldova
faced illicit financing, disinformation,
cyber attacks, and vote buying. Russia
spent the equivalent of nearly 2% of our
GDP trying to influence last year's
elections.
Muldovans answered that the home is not
for sale. Each of these choices carried
a cost, but each taught us the same
lesson. We cannot control everything
around us, but what we do still matters.
That is the source of our optimism. Our
future remains in our hands and nowhere
is that choice clearer today than in our
European path. European integration has
become our national project. Muldova has
been a candidate country since 2022.
Accession negotiations are underway and
we are moving quickly. Our ambition is
clear to anchor Muldova firmly in the
European family. For us, joining the
European Union is not about replacing
one sphere of influence with another. It
is the opposite. It is our citizens
exercising their right to choose. Choose
democracy, choose prosperity, choose
peace.
The European choice goes handinhand with
a strong transatlantic partnership. For
Muldova, these are not competing
directions. The United States has been
an important partner in strengthening
our security, energy independence, and
resilience. We want the next chapter of
that relationship to be increasingly
about trade, investment, technology, and
building things together.
But membership is not only about what
Europe can give Muldova. It is also
about what Muldova can bring. A
democracy that has learned to resist
interference,
an emerging economy, a country
contributing to stability on Europe's
eastern frontier, and a small state
willing to experiment, reform, and move
quickly.
Being small imposes constraints, but can
it can also be an advantage. Mulova is
not a huge domestic market. We cannot
outspend the largest economies. So we
have to compete differently with permits
in days rather than months. Clear
regulation, digital public services and
rules that change when they no longer
make sense. Technology is moving faster
than regulation almost everywhere and
artificial intelligence is widening that
gap. Small countries can have a natural
edge here. We want Moldova to become a
place where emerging technologies can be
tested responsibly through regulatory
sandboxes, where regulators learn
alongside companies, rules adjust with
evidence, and good ideas do not wait
years to reach the real economy. When an
entrepreneur arrives with a technology
for which the law has not caught up yet,
the answer should not simply be there is
no rule for this. It should be let us
find a safe way to test it. We may never
have the deepest pools of capital or the
largest GPU clusters, but we can build
better rules and be more agile.
Smallness does not have to mean
weakness. Sometimes it means turning
faster and delivering when larger
countries cannot. And that leads to a
broader point about small nations.
Power has never been equal. It never
will be. But inequality of power must
never become inequality of sovereignty.
Countries are not buffers. Nations are
not bargaining chiefs. Safety is not
abstract to me. Ke was home for nearly
15 years, including on that fateful
morning of 24th of February, 2022.
That morning, as parents, we struggled
to explain to our three boys at the
time, 1, 10, and 12, what war actually
meant. Perhaps nothing captures the
normalization of this war better than
the arithmetic children have learned.
Think of a typical night. A jet powered
Chahed drone is reported towards Kief. A
12-year-old checks the map, knows
roughly how fast it is traveling, and
does the math in his head. Perhaps 40
more minutes.
40 more minutes of sleep before
approaching drones sends him to the bomb
shelter. Children have become
frighteningly good at this. The nightly
arithmetic of war. In Muldova, we cannot
begin to compare our suffering with
Ukraines. Yet Russian drones have
repeatedly violated our airspace and
fallen in our territory. The danger is
that the unacceptable starts to feel
normal. For us too, this is about the
safety of our families. We must not grow
accustomed to it. Repetition does not
make violation acceptable. And because
these are not abstract questions for
Muldovans watching at home, allow me to
speak to them directly for a moment.
>> My fellow Muldovans, I know many of you
are anxiously following the news about
the war next door and the growing threat
from Russian drones and are already
thinking about the winter ahead.
Yes,
a difficult winter awaits us. Our duty
as a government is to prepare and to
help those
who need it most.
That is what we are working on and that
is what we are discussing with our
partners here.
But I want to ask something important of
you. Let us stick together
in difficult times. This is what has
always helped us through. being there
for one another, helping our neighbors,
our parents, and those struggling the
most. We may hold different views. We
may vote differently.
That is a that is natural in a country
where people think freely, but caring
for those around us must unite us.
We are a small country that makes it all
the more important
to know that we are not alone
>> and that we can count on one another.
>> That solidarity at home must go hand in
hand with clarity about the danger
around us. This is not a tragedy without
an author. Russia launched a war of
aggression against a sovereign neighbor.
It occupied territory and continued to
attack Ukrainian cities. Ukraine did not
choose this war. Russia did. We often
speak about war fatigue. The phrase is
understandable. Governments have other
crisis. Families have their own worries.
Attention moves on. But being tired of a
war you can switch off is different from
being tired because of an air raid wakes
your children at night. and different
still from the exhaustion of Ukrainian
soldiers spending another cold night in
the mud.
Muldova could not choose that this war
began next to us. But we could choose
our response. We welcomed people fleeing
the war. We kept transport routes open.
We reduce the cost of rail transit for
Ukrainian cargo with grain. These
decisions were not always costf free or
politically easy at home. We made them
because the way this war ends matters to
us far beyond our region. If aggression
is rewarded, it becomes a precedent for
the aggressor and for everyone watching.
Peace must protect sovereignty and
create the conditions for lasting
security. The same principle applies
within our own borders. Russian military
forces remain illegally and without our
consent in the Transistrian region of
Muldova. We will continue to seek their
unconditional withdrawal and the
peaceful reintegration of our country.
With full respect for Muldova
sovereignty and territorial integrity,
we want people on both banks of the
Nistro to live together in a peaceful,
democratic and prosperous Muldova. And
because we believe small states should
help shape the international system, not
simply depend on it, Muldova is honored
to present its candidacy for the
presidency of the 82nd session of the
United Nations General Assembly.
We want to contribute to a UN that is
more effective, more inclusive, and
focused on results.
We live in a world with plenty of
reasons for pessimism. Muldova chooses
something else. Not naive optimism, not
the belief that problems disappear if we
refuse to see them. The optimism that
comes from knowing that our future is
still in our hands. For too long,
Muldoans were told that our country was
too small, too exposed, too divided to
choose its own future. We have spent
enough time believing that. We know our
problems, but we should also know our
strength. We are a free country. Our
people are humble, work hard, and put
family first. Our diaspora is spread
across the world, but stays close to one
another and deeply cares about what
happens at home. Only when it comes to
vineyards does modesty become a little
harder for us. We quietly suspect our
wines might just be the best in the
world. We have friends across Europe,
across Atlantic, and far beyond. and we
finally have a realistic path to build a
country our children should not need to
leave in search of opportunity.
Muldova may never be a great power but
we have everything it takes to be a
great country. Thank you.
I on behalf of the assembly I wish to
thank the prime minister of the Republic
of Moldova.
